guide.what: Pronouns are short words that replace a noun so you don't repeat it: yo, lo, le, me, esto, alguien, que. Spanish has different forms depending on the job the word does in the sentence (subject, object, after a preposition, etc.).

rules.d: The verb ending already shows who does the action, so yo, tú, él are often left out. Use them only for emphasis, contrast or to avoid confusion.
rules.ex: Trabajo en Panamá, pero ella trabaja en Costa Rica.
rules.exEn: I work in Panama, but she works in Costa Rica.

rules.d: Usted is the polite 'you' and takes a third-person verb (usted tiene). For more than one person, Latin America uses ustedes for everyone, friends or strangers.
rules.exEn: Ma'am, do you have an appointment? Guys, are you coming?

rules.d: Put me, te, lo, la, le, se, nos, les before a conjugated verb. Attach them to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command. With 'verb + infinitive' both positions work. Negative commands: pronoun before the verb.
rules.ex: Lo quiero comprar. / Quiero comprarlo. ¡Cómpralo! No lo compres.
rules.exEn: I want to buy it. Buy it! Don't buy it.

rules.d: When there are two object pronouns, the indirect one (to whom) comes first: me lo, te la, nos los. A reflexive se always goes first of all.
rules.exEn: The photo? He sent it to me yesterday.

rules.t: Le and les become se before lo/la
rules.d: Never say 'le lo' or 'les la'. Change le/les to se, then add a + person if you need to be clear.
rules.ex: ¿Las llaves? Se las di a tu papá.
rules.exEn: The keys? I gave them to your dad.

rules.d: After a preposition use mí, ti, sí (para mí, de ti). With con use conmigo, contigo, consigo. Exception: entre, según and excepto take yo and tú.
rules.ex: Entre tú y yo, no quiero ir contigo.
rules.exEn: Between you and me, I don't want to go with you.

rules.t: Choosing que, quien, el que, lo que
rules.d: Que is the default for people and things. Use quien or el que after a preposition (con quien, en el que). Use lo que for 'what' or for a whole idea.
rules.ex: El amigo con quien viajé me dijo lo que pasó.
rules.exEn: The friend I traveled with told me what happened.

rules.d: Qué, quién, cuál, cuánto (and dónde, cómo) carry an accent in direct and indirect questions and in exclamations. The same words without accent are relatives or conjunctions.
rules.ex: No sé qué quiere. Dice que viene.
rules.exEn: I don't know what he wants. He says that he's coming.

rules.t: Doubling the indirect object is normal
rules.d: Spanish often uses le/les and also names the person with a: Le di el libro a Ana. With gustar-type verbs, add a mí, a ti for emphasis, never instead of the pronoun.
rules.ex: A mí me encanta el ceviche.

mistakes.why: With gustar the thing liked is the subject; you are the indirect object me.
Le/les change to se before lo, la, los, las.
Use the pronoun once: before the verb or attached, not both.

mistakes.wrong: El hombre yo vi es mi vecino.
mistakes.right: El hombre que vi es mi vecino.
mistakes.why: Spanish never drops the relative que.
'What' in the middle of a sentence is lo que (or qué in an indirect question).

items.use: The most common relative word: links a description to a noun, for people or things. Never leave it out like English 'the car I bought'.
items.ex: El carro que compré es rojo.
items.exEn: The car (that) I bought is red.

items.use: Reflexive for él, ella, usted, ellos, ustedes. Goes before a conjugated verb, or attached to an infinitive, gerund or affirmative command (levántese).
items.ex: Ella se levanta a las seis.
items.exEn: She gets up at six.

items.use: Replaces a masculine direct object. Before a conjugated verb (lo compré); attached to infinitive, gerund or affirmative command (cómpralo).
items.ex: ¿El celular? Lo dejé en la casa.
items.exEn: The phone? I left it at home.
items.latam: In Spain many people say le for a man (le vi = I saw him). In Latin America use lo.

items.use: Replaces a feminine direct object. Same placement as lo. Don't confuse it with the article la (la casa).
items.exEn: The key? I can't find it.

items.use: Object form of yo. Before a conjugated verb (me llamó); attached to infinitive, gerund or affirmative command (llámame).
items.exEn: My mom called me last night.

items.use: Indirect object for one person. Often doubled with a + noun: Le di el regalo a Ana. Changes to se before lo, la, los, las.
items.ex: Le escribí un mensaje a mi jefe.
items.exEn: I wrote my boss a message.

items.use: Usually dropped because the verb already shows the person (hablo = I speak). Use it for emphasis or contrast.
items.exEn: I'll pay this time.

items.use: Always has an accent in questions, also indirect ones (No sé qué hacer). Use qué + ser to ask for a definition (¿Qué es esto?).
items.exEn: What do you want to eat today?

items.use: Use for 'what' in the middle of a sentence, or for an idea with no noun. Plain que is wrong here.
items.exEn: I don't understand what you're saying.

items.use: The accent separates él (he) from el (the). Often dropped; use it to make clear who you mean.
items.exEn: He works at a bank.

items.use: Neuter: for ideas, situations or unknown things, never for a person. Never has an accent.
items.exEn: That's not true.

items.use: Object form of tú. Same placement rules as me: before a conjugated verb, attached to infinitive, gerund or affirmative command.
items.exEn: I'll call you later.

items.use: Object form of nosotros/nosotras. Before a conjugated verb or attached (invitarnos).
items.exEn: They invited us to the wedding.

items.use: Often dropped, but used more than yo or tú because the verb form doesn't show he vs. she.
items.exEn: She lives in David.

items.use: Indirect object plural, for ellos, ellas and ustedes. Changes to se before lo, la, los, las (se lo di).
items.ex: Les mandé las fotos a mis primos.
items.exEn: I sent the photos to my cousins.

items.use: Indirect object of yo. Very common with gustar-type verbs: me gusta, me duele, me encanta.
items.exEn: Can you pass me the salt?

items.use: With an accent tú = you; without, tu = your. Takes the tú verb form (tú hablas). Often dropped.
items.exEn: Are you from Panama?
items.latam: Panamanians use tú with friends and family. Vos is heard in parts of Central America and in rural western Panama.

items.use: Takes a third-person verb (usted habla, usted tiene). Use with strangers, older people, clients and at work. Written Ud.
items.exEn: Do you need help?
items.latam: In Panama usted is very common, even between neighbors and sometimes within families.

items.use: Neuter: for things you can't name yet or for ideas. Never for a person and never with an accent.
items.exEn: What's this?

items.use: Used with reflexive verbs: me levanto, me baño, me llamo. Same placement as other object pronouns (voy a levantarme).
items.exEn: My name is Carlos.

items.en: (to) him, her, you, them (instead of le/les)
items.use: Le and les become se before lo, la, los, las. Never say 'le lo'. Order: se + lo/la.
items.ex: ¿El libro? Se lo di a María.
items.exEn: The book? I gave it to María.

items.use: After the verb it needs no: No quiero nada. Before the verb, no 'no': Nada funciona.
items.exEn: I have nothing to do.

items.use: Use in positive sentences and questions. In negative sentences switch to nada.
items.exEn: Do you want something to drink?

items.use: As a direct object it usually adds lo: Lo sé todo. Lo entiendo todo.
items.exEn: Everything is ready.

items.use: Replaces a plural masculine or mixed direct object; also ustedes as object. Same placement as lo.
items.exEn: The tickets? I bought them yesterday.

items.use: Always has an accent in questions. Use quiénes for more than one. With a preposition: ¿Con quién? ¿De quién?
items.exEn: Who's that man?

items.use: Use after prepositions: para mí, a mí, de mí. Accent: mí = me, mi = my. With con it becomes conmigo.
items.exEn: Is this gift for me?

items.use: Indirect object of tú. Common with gustar: ¿Te gusta? Before lo/la stays te: te lo doy.
items.exEn: I brought you a coffee.

items.use: Reflexive for tú: te levantas, te llamas. Attached to commands: ¡Siéntate!
items.exEn: What time do you get up?

items.use: se + third-person singular verb for general statements, rules and signs, with no specific person.
items.exEn: Spanish is spoken here.

items.use: Use nosotras if the group is all female. Usually dropped (vamos = we go).
items.exEn: We're going by car.

items.use: Takes a third-person plural verb (ustedes hablan). In Latin America it is the only plural 'you', formal or informal.
items.exEn: Do you all want to come?
items.latam: Spain uses vosotros for friends and ustedes only for formal plural. In Panama use ustedes for everyone.

items.use: Use for men or a mixed group. Usually dropped (llegan = they arrive).
items.exEn: They arrive tomorrow.

items.use: Replaces a plural feminine direct object. Same placement as la.
items.exEn: The keys? I have them.

items.use: Use after prepositions: para ti, a ti, de ti. No accent on ti. With con it becomes contigo.
items.exEn: This is for you.

items.use: For people, mostly after a preposition (con quien) or between commas. Without a preposition, que is more natural.
items.ex: La persona con quien hablé fue muy amable.
items.exEn: The person I spoke with was very kind.

items.use: Agrees with the noun it replaces. Modern spelling has no accent (éste is the old spelling).
items.exEn: Which one do you want? —This one.

items.use: Very common to introduce people: Esta es mi hermana. No accent needed.
items.exEn: This is my sister Lucía.

items.use: For something near the listener or a bit away. In everyday speech it also covers 'that one over there'.
items.exEn: That one is my car.

items.use: Agrees with the feminine noun it replaces.
items.ex: No quiero esta camisa, quiero esa.
items.exEn: I don't want this shirt, I want that one.

items.use: Neuter lo replaces a whole idea or an adjective: Lo sé. ¿Es caro? —Sí, lo es.
items.exEn: I don't know.

items.use: After the verb add no: No vino nadie. Before the verb no 'no': Nadie vino. Takes personal a as object: No vi a nadie.
items.ex: No hay nadie en la oficina.
items.exEn: There's nobody in the office.

items.use: Use in positive sentences and questions. As an object it takes personal a: Busco a alguien.
items.exEn: Does anyone have a charger?

items.use: Use to choose among options, and with ser for 'What is your...?' (¿Cuál es tu número?), not qué.
items.exEn: What's your cell number?

items.use: Only for a group that is all female; any man in the group makes it ellos.
items.exEn: They study at the university.

items.use: Indirect object of nosotros. Before lo/la it stays nos: nos lo dieron.
items.exEn: They gave us a discount.

items.use: Reflexive or 'each other' for nosotros: nos levantamos, nos vemos.
items.exEn: See you tomorrow.

items.use: With plural verbs se can mean 'each other' (reciprocal). Context tells you if it means themselves or each other.
items.exEn: They love each other a lot.

items.use: Never put un before it: otro, not 'un otro'.
items.exEn: This one doesn't work, give me another.

items.use: Plural verb: Todos están. Todas for an all-female group.
items.exEn: Everyone is invited.

items.use: For general statements about anyone, like English 'you' or 'one'. Also 'one' of a group (uno de ellos).
items.exEn: You never know.

items.use: Special form: never say 'con mí'.
items.exEn: Do you want to go to the movies with me?

items.use: Special form: never say 'con ti'. For usted say con usted.
items.exEn: I'll talk to you tomorrow.

items.use: Agrees with the noun. Needed after prepositions (en el que, con el que) and for 'the one who'.
items.ex: Mi hermano es el que vive en Colón.
items.exEn: My brother is the one who lives in Colón.

items.use: Feminine form of el que; common after prepositions.
items.ex: La casa en la que crecí ya no existe.
items.exEn: The house I grew up in no longer exists.

items.use: Plural of el que. Often with subjunctive for people not yet known.
items.exEn: Those who want to come, let me know.

items.use: Plural feminine of el que.
items.ex: De todas las playas, estas son las que más me gustan.
items.exEn: Of all the beaches, these are the ones I like most.

items.use: As a relative it has no accent. Only ¿dónde? in questions has one.
items.ex: Esta es la ciudad donde nací.
items.exEn: This is the city where I was born.

items.use: Only when the whole group is female.
items.exEn: We're coworkers.

items.use: Plural of este. Use for things or people near you.
items.exEn: These are my children.

items.use: Plural of esta.
items.ex: De todas las fotos, estas son las mejores.
items.exEn: Of all the photos, these are the best.

items.use: Plural of ese.
items.exEn: Those are my shoes.

items.use: Plural of esa.
items.exEn: How much do those cost?

items.use: Alone use alguno; before a noun it shortens to algún. Often with de: alguno de ustedes.
items.exEn: Do any of you speak English?

items.use: Plural, very common for 'some people'.
items.ex: Algunos prefieren trabajar desde la casa.
items.exEn: Some prefer to work from home.

items.use: Feminine of alguno.
items.exEn: Do any of your friends live nearby?

items.use: Feminine plural of alguno.
items.ex: Tengo muchas camisas, pero algunas ya no me quedan.
items.exEn: I have lots of shirts, but some don't fit me anymore.

items.use: Alone ninguno; before a noun ningún. After the verb add no: No vino ninguno.
items.ex: No vino ninguno de mis amigos.
items.exEn: None of my friends came.

items.use: Feminine of ninguno. Normally singular.
items.exEn: Do you have questions? —No, none.

items.use: Agrees with the noun. As an object it adds la: se la comieron toda.
items.exEn: And the pizza? —They ate all of it.

items.use: Feminine plural of todo.
items.exEn: They all arrived early.

items.use: Never 'una otra'.
items.ex: Esta talla no me queda, ¿tiene otra?
items.exEn: This size doesn't fit, do you have another?

items.use: Often paired with unos: unos... otros (some... others).
items.ex: Unos llegaron temprano y otros tarde.
items.exEn: Some arrived early and others late.

items.use: With the article: las otras = the other ones.
items.ex: Me gustan estas flores más que las otras.
items.exEn: I like these flowers more than the others.

items.use: Always with los (or lo demás = the rest of things).
items.ex: Yo me quedo; los demás se pueden ir.
items.exEn: I'm staying; the rest can go.

items.use: Neuter: refers to a thing or idea. Very common when ordering food.
items.exEn: The same for me.

items.use: As a pronoun it stands for 'a lot of things'. Mucho que + infinitive = a lot to do.
items.exEn: I have a lot to do today.

items.use: Plural for 'many people' or 'many of them'.
items.exEn: Many people think it's expensive.

items.use: Feminine plural of mucho.
items.exEn: Do you have female friends in Panama? —Yes, many.

items.use: Poco = not much (negative feeling); un poco = a little (positive).
items.exEn: I know little about politics.

items.use: Plural for 'few people' or 'few of them'.
items.exEn: Few people know the truth.

items.use: Takes a singular verb. Cada una for feminine.
items.ex: Cada uno trae algo de comer.
items.exEn: Each person brings something to eat.

items.use: Plural only. Varias for feminine.
items.ex: Varios de mis compañeros viven cerca.
items.exEn: Several of my coworkers live nearby.

items.use: A bit formal; in speech los dos is more common. Ambas for feminine.
items.exEn: Both of them are right.

items.use: Alone use cualquiera; before a noun it shortens to cualquier.
items.exEn: Anyone can learn to swim.

items.use: Accent in questions. Agrees with what you count: cuánto, cuánta, cuántos, cuántas.
items.exEn: How much does it cost?
items.latam: In Panama you'll often hear ¿Cuánto es? at the store.

items.use: Plural masculine; agrees with the noun you are counting.
items.exEn: How many are there in your family?

items.use: For a feminine uncountable noun (agua, harina, gente).
items.exEn: I need flour. —How much?

items.use: Plural feminine.
items.exEn: I bought empanadas. —How many?

items.use: Use when you expect more than one person in the answer.
items.exEn: Who's coming to the party?

items.use: Plural of cuál. Use with ser for 'What are your...?'.
items.exEn: What are your favorite movies?

items.use: Plural of relative quien, for people, mostly between commas or after a preposition.
items.ex: Mis vecinos, quienes son muy amables, me ayudaron.
items.exEn: My neighbors, who are very kind, helped me.

items.use: Formal, mostly written, after prepositions or commas. Same as el que.
items.ex: El edificio, frente al cual hay un parque, es nuevo.
items.exEn: The building, in front of which there's a park, is new.

items.use: Feminine of el cual. Common after prepositions in formal writing.
items.ex: La empresa para la cual trabajo es panameña.
items.exEn: The company I work for is Panamanian.

items.use: Plural of el cual.
items.ex: Compré dos libros, los cuales ya leí.
items.exEn: I bought two books, which I've already read.

items.use: Feminine plural of el cual. Very common in 'las razones por las cuales'.
items.ex: Hay varias razones por las cuales no fui.
items.exEn: There are several reasons why I didn't go.

items.use: Refers back to a whole sentence, after a comma. Lo que works the same way.
items.ex: Llegó tarde, lo cual me molestó.
items.exEn: He arrived late, which annoyed me.

items.use: Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner. Mostly formal or written.
items.ex: Es el autor cuyo libro leímos.
items.exEn: He's the author whose book we read.

items.use: Feminine because the thing owned is feminine (hija).
items.ex: Conocí a una mujer cuya hija estudia conmigo.
items.exEn: I met a woman whose daughter studies with me.

items.use: Agrees with the plural thing owned.
items.ex: Ese es el señor cuyos hijos juegan fútbol.
items.exEn: That's the man whose kids play soccer.

items.use: Agrees with the feminine plural thing owned.
items.ex: Es una empresa cuyas oficinas están en la Ciudad de Panamá.
items.exEn: It's a company whose offices are in Panama City.

items.use: For things far from both speaker and listener, or the distant past. Less common in speech than ese.
items.ex: Este carro es mío y aquel es de mi papá.
items.exEn: This car is mine and that one is my dad's.

items.use: Feminine of aquel.
items.ex: ¿Ves esa casa? No, aquella, la azul.
items.exEn: See that house? No, that one over there, the blue one.

items.use: Neuter, for something distant in time or space. Never for a person.
items.ex: ¿Te acuerdas de aquello que pasó en la universidad?
items.exEn: Do you remember that thing that happened in college?

items.use: Plural of aquel. Common for the past: aquellos años.
items.ex: Aquellos fueron los mejores años de mi vida.
items.exEn: Those were the best years of my life.

items.use: Plural of aquella.
items.ex: Estas naranjas son más dulces que aquellas.
items.exEn: These oranges are sweeter than those.

items.use: Article + possessive, agreeing with the thing owned, not the owner.
items.ex: Tu celular es más nuevo que el mío.
items.exEn: Your phone is newer than mine.

items.use: Agrees with the feminine thing owned.
items.ex: Tu casa es más grande que la mía.
items.exEn: Your house is bigger than mine.

items.use: Agrees with the plural thing owned. Los míos can also mean 'my family'.
items.ex: ¿Estos zapatos son tuyos? —No, los míos son negros.
items.exEn: Are these shoes yours? —No, mine are black.

items.use: Agrees with the feminine plural thing owned.
items.ex: Esas llaves no son las mías.
items.exEn: Those keys aren't mine.

items.use: For tú. Agrees with the thing owned.
items.ex: Mi carro está dañado; ¿me prestas el tuyo?
items.exEn: My car is broken; can you lend me yours?

items.use: Feminine form for tú.
items.ex: Mi idea es buena, pero la tuya es mejor.
items.exEn: My idea is good, but yours is better.

items.use: Plural form for tú.
items.ex: Mis hijos y los tuyos van a la misma escuela.
items.exEn: My kids and yours go to the same school.

items.use: Feminine plural form for tú.
items.ex: Mis llaves no abren; prueba con las tuyas.
items.exEn: My keys don't work; try yours.

items.use: Can mean many owners. To be clear, say el de él, el de ella, el de usted, el de ellos.
items.ex: Mi vuelo sale a las ocho; el suyo, a las diez.
items.exEn: My flight leaves at eight; his, at ten.

items.use: Feminine form; very common for polite 'yours' with usted.
items.ex: Esta no es mi maleta; es la suya, señora.
items.exEn: This isn't my suitcase; it's yours, ma'am.

items.use: Plural form. Also means 'his/her people, family'.
items.ex: Todos trajeron sus documentos, pero ella olvidó los suyos.
items.exEn: Everyone brought their documents, but she forgot hers.

items.use: Feminine plural form.
items.ex: Mis notas son buenas, pero las suyas son excelentes.
items.exEn: My grades are good, but hers are excellent.

items.use: For nosotros. Agrees with the thing owned.
items.ex: Su apartamento es más caro que el nuestro.
items.exEn: Their apartment is more expensive than ours.

items.use: Feminine form for nosotros.
items.ex: ¿De quién es esta mesa? —Es la nuestra.
items.exEn: Whose table is this? —It's ours.

items.use: Plural form. Also 'our people, our team'.
items.ex: Sus precios son altos; los nuestros, no.
items.exEn: Their prices are high; ours aren't.

items.use: Feminine plural form.
items.ex: Estas maletas no son las nuestras.
items.exEn: These suitcases aren't ours.

items.use: After ser the article is usually dropped: es mío, es mía, son míos. Still agrees with the thing.
items.exEn: That umbrella is mine.

items.use: After ser, no article: es tuyo, es tuya.
items.exEn: Is this phone yours?

items.use: After ser, no article. With usted it is the polite 'yours'.
items.exEn: Sir, is this umbrella yours?

items.use: Neuter lo + possessive = one's things, business or talent.
items.exEn: Cooking isn't my thing.

items.use: Neuter form for tú: your talent, your business.
items.exEn: Music is your thing.

items.use: Neuter form: hacer lo suyo = do one's own thing.
items.ex: Le gusta hacer lo suyo sin pedir ayuda.
items.exEn: She likes to do her own thing without asking for help.

items.use: Neuter form; often means a relationship.
items.ex: Lo nuestro terminó hace un año.
items.exEn: What we had ended a year ago.

items.use: Takes a singular verb even though it means many people.
items.exEn: Everybody knows that.

items.use: As a pronoun, often paired with otros: unos dicen... otros dicen.
items.ex: Unos dicen que sí y otros que no.
items.exEn: Some say yes and others say no.

items.use: Feminine plural of poco.
items.exEn: Are many stores open? —No, few.

items.use: Replaces tú in Argentina, Uruguay and much of Central America, with its own verb forms (vos sos, vos tenés). Its object form is te.
items.exEn: Are you from here?
items.latam: In Panama vos is heard mostly in rural areas of the west, like parts of Chiriquí and Veraguas. In the city use tú.

items.use: Spain only, with its own verb forms (habláis, tenéis). Learn to recognize it for DELE reading and listening.
items.exEn: Are you guys coming to the party?
items.latam: Never used in Panama or Latin America; say ustedes.

items.use: Spain only, for an all-female group.
items.exEn: Are you two sisters?

items.use: Spain only: direct, indirect and reflexive object of vosotros. Before a conjugated verb or attached.
items.exEn: I'll call you all tomorrow.
items.latam: In Latin America: Los llamo mañana / Les digo / Se levantan.

items.use: Spain only (also la vuestra, los vuestros). In Latin America say el suyo or el de ustedes.
items.ex: Nuestro piso es más pequeño que el vuestro.
items.exEn: Our apartment is smaller than yours.
items.latam: Latin America: Nuestro apartamento es más pequeño que el de ustedes.

items.use: Reflexive form after a preposition, often with mismo: para sí mismo. Needs the accent (si = if).
items.exEn: He talks a lot about himself.

items.use: Only when the person is the same as the subject. For another person use con él / con ella.
items.exEn: She always carries her phone with her.

items.use: Leísmo: in Spain le is often used instead of lo for a man or for usted. Recognize it, but in Latin America use lo.
items.ex: Le vi ayer en el banco.
items.exEn: I saw him yesterday at the bank.
items.latam: In Panama say: Lo vi ayer en el banco.

items.use: se + me/te/le + verb for accidents: the thing 'happened to' you. The verb agrees with the thing.
items.exEn: I forgot my keys.

items.use: Passive se: the verb agrees with the thing. Common on signs: se vende, se alquilan.
items.exEn: Apartment for rent.

items.use: Neuter, mostly in writing and after prepositions: por ello, para ello, de ello.
items.ex: Por ello, decidimos cancelar el viaje.
items.exEn: For that reason, we decided to cancel the trip.

items.use: A woman talking about people in general often uses una instead of uno.
items.ex: Una nunca sabe qué va a pasar.
items.exEn: You never know what's going to happen.

items.use: As a pronoun = too many things. Demasiados = too many (people/things).
items.ex: No quiero más, ya tengo demasiado.
items.exEn: I don't want more, I already have too much.

items.use: Plural bastantes. Means both 'enough' and 'quite a lot'.
items.exEn: You've already done plenty for me.

items.use: Agrees: tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas.
items.exEn: I don't need that much.

items.use: Accent in exclamations too: ¡Qué calor! ¡Qué bonito! In Panama you hear it constantly.
items.exEn: It's so hot today!

items.use: More formal or literary than cada uno. Singular verb.
items.exEn: Everyone has their own tastes.

items.use: Formal; followed by que + subjunctive.
items.ex: Quienquiera que sea, dile que no estoy.
items.exEn: Whoever it is, tell them I'm not here.
